overview: Both describe changes in DNA sequence, but they differ mainly in how common the variant is in a population.
genZNote: Rare change: mutation. Change so common it's basically just 'normal variety': polymorphism.

aspects.label: Population Frequency
aspects.valueA: Typically rare, often below 1% frequency in the population.
aspects.valueB: Common variant present in more than 1% of the population.

aspects.label: Typical Effect
aspects.valueA: Can be harmful, neutral, or (rarely) beneficial.
aspects.valueB: Usually neutral, contributing to normal variation like blood groups or eye colour.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: A new disease-causing mutation in a single family.
aspects.valueB: ABO blood group alleles or common SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms).

aspects.label: Origin
aspects.valueA: Can arise spontaneously or be induced by mutagens at any time.
aspects.valueB: Often a mutation that became established and common over many generations.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: A polymorphism is really just a mutation that succeeded population-wide — the 1% frequency cutoff is the operational definition.
overlay.memoryTrick: Poly = many, so polymorphism means many people carry it.
overlay.commonMisconception: Polymorphism does not mean 'harmless' by definition — some polymorphisms do have modest health effects, they are simply common.
